reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive deficiency of mitochondrial short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase (ECHS1 gene), an enzyme acting in valine catabolism and fatty-acid oxidation
Characteristically causes a Leigh or Leigh-like syndrome with developmental regression, dystonia, and symmetrical basal ganglia lesions on MRI
Presentation is often in infancy or early childhood, frequently with regression triggered or worsened by intercurrent illness
The mechanism is thought to involve accumulation of toxic valine-pathway intermediates rather than simple energy failure, which has prompted interest in valine (protein) restriction
Biochemical markers can be subtle, but urine organic acids may show metabolites such as 2-methyl-2,3-dihydroxybutyrate and S-(2-carboxypropyl)cysteine derivatives; lactate may be raised
ECHS1 deficiency is an important, potentially treatable cause of Leigh-like disease that can be missed if only the respiratory chain is investigated
Management is largely supportive, with dietary valine/protein restriction and avoidance of catabolic stress explored as disease-modifying approaches
reference.pathophysiology: Short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase (ECHS1, crotonase) catalyses hydration of short-chain enoyl-CoA esters and participates in the catabolism of the branched-chain amino acid valine as well as in fatty-acid beta-oxidation. Deficiency is believed to cause disease predominantly through accumulation of reactive valine-pathway intermediates (such as methacrylyl-CoA and acryloyl-CoA derivatives) that damage mitochondrial proteins, producing a Leigh-like encephalopathy with characteristic basal ganglia injury. Secondary impairment of energy metabolism, with lactate elevation, may accompany this. Because the toxic intermediates arise chiefly from valine, restricting valine intake is a rational, if still investigational, strategy.
additionalDifferentials: Leigh syndrome from mitochondrial DNA or nuclear respiratory chain defects
Biotinidase and biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease
Other organic acidaemias causing basal ganglia injury
3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA hydrolase (HIBCH) deficiency in the same valine pathway
Acquired or hypoxic-ischaemic basal ganglia injury
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to identify symmetrical basal ganglia and brainstem lesions
Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate measurement
Urine organic acids for valine-pathway metabolites (e.g. 2-methyl-2,3-dihydroxybutyrate)
Plasma acylcarnitine and amino acid profiles
ECHS1 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Enzyme activity or functional studies in fibroblasts where genetics are inconclusive
redFlags: Developmental regression with new dystonia or movement disorder
Acute neurological deterioration during intercurrent illness
Progressive Leigh-like lesions on serial imaging
Feeding difficulties, respiratory compromise or brainstem dysfunction
reference.prognosis: The disorder is frequently severe and progressive, with a Leigh-like course and significant neurological disability or early death in classic cases; milder phenotypes exist, and valine/protein restriction is being studied as a potential disease-modifying measure.
pitfalls: Attributing Leigh-like disease solely to a respiratory chain defect and not testing ECHS1
Being reassured by subtle or near-normal routine metabolic screening
Overlooking the related valine-pathway disorder HIBCH with a similar presentation
Failing to consider dietary valine restriction as a potentially modifying intervention
references: Scriver's OMMBID: Disorders of Valine Metabolism and Leigh Syndrome
Saudubray, Baumgartner & Walter, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: Valine (protein) restriction as an investigational disease-modifying strategy to limit accumulation of toxic valine-pathway intermediates
Avoidance of catabolic stress with an emergency regimen providing carbohydrate and energy during intercurrent illness
Supportive treatment of dystonia with agents such as trihexyphenidyl, baclofen, or a levodopa trial, alongside physiotherapy
A mitochondrial supportive cocktail (thiamine, riboflavin, coenzyme Q10) as adjunctive care
Anticonvulsants for seizures and management of feeding difficulty, with gastrostomy where needed
Neurodevelopmental support and multidisciplinary rehabilitation for disability
Surveillance with brain MRI and lactate monitoring, and prompt management of acute metabolic or neurological decompensation
Genetic counselling and family testing for the autosomal recessive ECHS1 defect
